topic: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) - KDIGO Definition and Staging
content: AKI (acute kidney injury): abrupt decline in renal function. KDIGO criteria: ≥1.5× increase in creatinine within 7 days OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6-12 hours. Stage 1: 1.5-1.9× Cr, output <0.5 mL/kg/hr x 6-8h. Stage 2: 2.0-2.9× Cr, output <0.5 mL/kg/hr x 16h. Stage 3: ≥3× Cr or Cr ≥4 or initiation RRT, output <0.3 mL/kg/hr x 24h. Mortality increases with AKI stage: 2-5% Stage 1, 5-10% Stage 2, 15-25% Stage 3. Risk factors: age, CKD, diabetes, hypotension, nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, ACE-I/ARBs in certain settings, aminoglycosides, contrast).

Prerenal AKI: hypoperfusion to kidneys (hypovolemia, sepsis, cardiogenic shock, renal artery stenosis). Incidence 55-70% of AKI. Pathophysiology: reduced glomerular filtration pressure -> oliguria, preserved tubular function. Diagnosis: FeNa <1% (fractional excretion sodium), urine osmolality >500, BUN/Cr ratio >20, urine sodium <20. Response to fluids rapidly (if prerenal). Risk: progression to ATN if prolonged hypoperfusion. Management: address underlying cause (restore volume, increase cardiac output, relieve obstruction), avoid nephrotoxins, avoid excessive fluids (risk pulmonary edema if cardiogenic shock).

Intrinsic AKI (25-30% of AKI): direct kidney injury. ATN (most common intrinsic AKI): tubular epithelial cell necrosis. Causes: hypotension/ischemia (ischemic ATN) or nephrotoxins (toxic ATN). Ischemic ATN: sepsis, cardiogenic shock, major surgery, rhabdomyolysis. Toxic ATN: aminoglycosides, cisplatin, myoglobin (rhabdo), hemoglobin (massive hemolysis), contrast (volume depletion risk), NSAIDs, ACE-I (in certain volume-depleted states). Diagnosis: FeNa >2%, muddy brown casts (myoglobin-stained), urine sodium >40. Recovery 7-21 days typically (tubule regeneration). Management: supportive (fluids, avoid further nephrotoxins), RRT if oliguria/electrolyte dysregulation. Oliguric ATN worse prognosis (mortality 50-60%) than non-oliguric (mortality 5-10%).

Postrenal AKI (5-10% of AKI): urinary tract obstruction distal to kidney. Causes: kidney stones, tumors, strictures, neurogenic bladder (spinal cord injury, cauda equina), BPH prostate obstruction, retroperitoneal fibrosis. Unilateral obstruction may not cause AKI (contralateral kidney compensates); bilateral obstruction required. Presentation: anuria (absent urine), flank pain (stones), suprapubic distension (bladder obstruction). Diagnosis: ultrasound (hydronephrosis), CT (stone, tumor), post-void residual volume (elevated in bladder obstruction). Management: catheterization (Foley or suprapubic) for bladder outlet obstruction, urology consultation for upper tract obstruction (stent, percutaneous nephrostomy). Outcomes: excellent if relief <1 week; delayed relief risk permanent renal dysfunction (tubular atrophy if prolonged).

topic: Urinalysis Interpretation in AKI - Casts and Crystals
content: Muddy brown casts: pathognomonic for ATN (myoglobin-stained tubular cells + Tamm-Horsfall protein), appear in ischemic/toxic ATN. RBC casts: indicate glomerulonephritis (RPGN/IGAN/PSGN/lupus). WBC casts: interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis. Hyaline casts: benign, concentrated urine. Crystals: calcium oxalate (star/dumbbell-shaped) = ethylene glycol toxicity, uric acid (diamond/rhomboid) = hyperuricemia/tumor lysis, urea nitrogen, sulfur (sulfadiazine crystals). Crystal-induced AKI requires aggressive fluids (urine output >200 mL/hr), urine alkalinization (some crystals), specific antidotes (fomepizole for ethylene glycol). Absence of casts doesn't exclude intrinsic AKI (10% have granular/epithelial cells only).

topic: Rhabdomyolysis and Myoglobinuria - AKI from Muscle Breakdown
content: Rhabdomyolysis: skeletal muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin (brown protein) into urine. Causes: crush injury, statins (rare but serious), alcohol, seizures, heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia. Presentation: brown/cola-colored urine (myoglobinuria), muscle pain, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia. AKI mechanism: myoglobin tubular precipitation, direct tubular toxicity. Risk factors for AKI in rhabdo: volume depletion, acidic urine (myoglobin precipitates better at low pH). Management: aggressive IV hydration (goal urine output 200-300 mL/hr, maintain intravascular volume), urine alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate (pH >6.5), avoid NSAIDs/ACE-I (worsen volume depletion). Monitor CK (peaks day 3), electrolytes (hyperkalemia), calcium (treat symptomatic hypocalcemia cautiously, risk metastatic calcification). RRT if oliguria/severe electrolyte dysregulation.

NSAIDs: inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reduce renal blood flow. Risk in volume-depleted states (heart failure, sepsis, cirrhosis), elderly, pre-existing CKD. ACE-I/ARBs: block angiotensin II (efferent arteriole vasoconstriction). Beneficial in proteinuric disease but harmful in volume depletion (loss of efferent arteriole tone = reduced GFR). Hold ACE-I/ARBs if: SBP <90, acute diarrhea/vomiting, acute AKI, renal artery stenosis. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin): concentrate in proximal tubule, dose-dependent & concentration-dependent nephrotoxicity. Risk: prolonged therapy, high trough levels, volume depletion, baseline CKD. Use extended-interval dosing (once-daily amikacin 15 mg/kg) reduces nephrotoxicity vs q8h dosing. Monitor: Cr, drug levels, BUN. Alternatives: fluoroquinolones if susceptible organism.

Contrast-induced nephropathy: AKI within 48-72h of iodinated contrast exposure. Risk: baseline CKD (GFR <60), diabetes, volume depletion, age >75, heart failure, multiple contrast exposures. Mechanism: direct tubular toxicity, osmotic injury, renal vasoconstriction. Prevention: IV hydration (0.9% NS 1 mL/kg/hr x 4-6 hours before + 6 hours after contrast; 3 mL/kg if LVEF <35), metformin hold 48h post-contrast (accumulation if AKI develops), aminoglycosides hold (additive nephrotoxicity). N-acetylcysteine controversial (prior evidence, later trials negative). Sodium bicarbonate vs isotonic saline: saline preferred (randomized trials show no superiority of bicarbonate). Management: monitor Cr at 48-72h, adjust medications if AKI develops.

topic: Renal Replacement Therapy (RRT) - CRRT vs Intermittent Hemodialysis
content: CRRT (continuous renal replacement therapy): low blood flow (150-200 mL/min), gradual fluid/solute removal. Advantages: hemodynamic stability in hypotensive patients, better metabolic control, allows nutrition. Disadvantages: immobilizes patient (ICU-bound), anticoagulation needs, expensive, staffing intensive. Indications: hypotension, need rapid fluid removal (not compatible with intermittent), electrolyte dysregulation (needs frequent adjustment). Intermittent hemodialysis: high blood flow (300-500 mL/min), rapid removal. Advantages: shorter duration, mobilizes patient, less anticoagulation. Disadvantages: hemodynamic instability (hypotension, arrhythmias) post-dialysis, slower electrolyte correction (risk rebound), less suited for hypotensive patients. Choice depends: clinical stability, hemodynamics, ICU capacity. CRRT preferred in sepsis/shock (hemodynamic instability); intermittent reasonable in stable AKI.

topic: RRT Indications - When to Start and Relative Contraindications
content: RRT indications (RIFLE/KDIGO based): (1) Refractory hyperkalemia (K+ >6.5 refractory to medical management). (2) Refractory pulmonary edema/fluid overload (oliguria, high fluid requirements). (3) Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1 refractory). (4) Uremia symptoms (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding). (5) Severe electrolyte abnormalities (hyponatremia, hypocalcemia unresponsive to treatment). Relative contraindications: hemodynamic instability (relative; CRRT preferred over intermittent), active bleeding (if anticoagulation for CRRT needed; heparin-free circuits possible), thrombocytopenia <50k (bleeding risk with anticoagulation). Early RRT (within 24-48h of AKI diagnosis) may improve outcomes in severe AKI (KDIGO 3) based on recent trials; avoid delay if indications present.

topic: Hyperkalemia - EKG Changes and Treatment Algorithm
content: Hyperkalemia: K+ >5.5 mEq/L. Symptoms: weakness, palpitations, syncope (rare until K+ >7). EKG changes (progressive): peaked T waves (K+ 5.5-6.5), prolonged PR/widened QRS (K+ 6.5-7.5), loss of P wave/bradycardia, sine wave (K+ >8, cardiac arrest imminent). Absent symptoms/EKG doesn't exclude danger (can progress rapidly). Management algorithm: (1) Calcium gluconate 10-20 mL of 10% IV bolus (cardiac membrane stabilization, no K+ lowering, 30-60 min duration). (2) Insulin 10 units IV + dextrose 25g (50 mL D50W) = shift K+ intracellularly, effect 10-20 min, lasts 4-6 hours. (3) Beta-2 agonist (albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized) = K+ shift, slower onset. (4) Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 amps IV (raises pH, K+ shift), use if acidemia. (5) Diuretics (furosemide) if euvolemic. (6) RRT if refractory/oliguric. (7) Cation exchange resin (kayexalate, sodium polystyrene sulfonate) = slow K+ removal via GI excretion.

Hyponatremia: Na+ <135 mEq/L. Classify by osmolality: hyperosmolar (hyperglycemia, mannitol, contrast), isosmolar (pseudohyponatremia from lipemia/proteinemia, now rare with direct Na+ measurement), hypoosmolar (true dilution). Hypoosmolar causes: SIADH (euvolemic, urine osmolality >100, urine Na+ >40), diuretics (hypovolemic, urine Na+ >20, low urine osmolality), heart failure/cirrhosis/nephrotic (hypervolemic). SIADH diagnosis: euvolemic hyponatremia, low serum osmolality (<280), high urine osmolality (>100), high urine Na+ (>40), normal renal/adrenal/thyroid function. Causes: CNS (meningitis, head trauma, seizures), pulmonary (infection, positive pressure ventilation), malignancy (lung cancer, SCLC), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, vincristine, MDMA), pain/stress.

topic: Symptomatic vs Asymptomatic Hyponatremia - Acute vs Chronic
content: Symptomatic hyponatremia: nausea, headache, confusion, lethargy, seizures (Na+ <120), coma, death (if severe <110). Acute hyponatremia (<48h): cells haven't adapted, increased intracellular fluid volume -> cerebral edema risk at lower Na+ levels. Chronic hyponatremia (>48h): osmolytes extruded from cells, cerebral edema less likely even if Na+ very low. Correction rate critical: too-rapid correction (>12 mEq/L in 24h) risks central pontine myelinolysis (demyelination, locked-in syndrome, death). Acute symptomatic: 3% hypertonic saline (NaCl 3%, 1 mL/kg IV bolus, repeat once if still seizing), aim for 4-6 mEq/L rise per hour. Chronic asymptomatic: fluid restriction (SIADH), slow correction 4-8 mEq/L per 24h.

topic: Hyponatremia Treatment - 3% Saline, Fluid Restriction, Vaptans
content: 3% hypertonic saline (NaCl 3%): reserved for symptomatic acute hyponatremia. Dosing: 1-2 mL/kg IV bolus (50-100 mL), repeat once after seizure cessation, then reassess. Calculate Na+ rise: change in Na+ = ([Na+ infused] - [Na+ serum]) / (total body water + 1). Example: 100 mL 3% saline (513 mEq/L) in 70 kg patient (TBW ~42L) = ~1 mEq/L rise. Fluid restriction: first-line for SIADH, restrict to 500-800 mL/day. Vaptans (tolvaptan, conivaptan): vasopressin antagonists, aquaretics (promote free water excretion). Used in SIADH refractory to fluid restriction; oral or IV. Caution: rapid Na+ correction risk, expensive, hepatotoxicity monitoring needed. Monitor: serum Na+ q2-4h during acute treatment, avoid hypernatremia (over-correction), neuro checks.

topic: Hypernatremia - Causes and Free Water Deficit Calculation
content: Hypernatremia: Na+ >145 mEq/L. Causes: insensible losses (diabetes insipidus, sweating, diarrhea, inadequate intake, hypertonic fluid administration. Diabetes insipidus (DI): central (pituitary damage/surgery, hypothyroidism, trauma, idiopathic) vs nephrogenic (congenital, lithium, hypercalcemia, CKD). Presentation: polyuria, polydipsia (if intact thirst), hypernatremia (if intake insufficient), hypertonicity symptoms (restlessness, confusion, lethargy). Free water deficit calculation: FWD (liters) = (0.6 × body weight kg × [(Na+ serum / 140) - 1]). Replacement: calculate rate to replace over 48 hours (slower than hyponatremia correction, risk cerebral edema). D5W or 0.45% NS. Treat underlying cause (vasopressin if central DI, NSAIDs/amiloride if nephrogenic DI).

topic: Correction Rate Calculations - Avoiding Osmotic Demyelination
content: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS): central pontine + extrapontine myelinolysis from overly rapid Na+ correction (>12 mEq/L in 24h). Risk: chronic hyponatremia (cells adapted), rapid correction re-creates osmotic gradient = cellular dehydration -> demyelination. Symptoms: flaccid paralysis, locked-in appearance, death (acute), behavioral changes/movement disorders (delayed recovery phase). Prevention: limit correction to 4-8 mEq/L per 24h (chronic) or 10-12 mEq/L per 24h (acute symptomatic). Monitor: serum Na+ q4-6h during acute correction, adjust infusion rate. If Na+ rising too fast: stop hypertonic saline, reduce rate, use dextrose (free water) to slow correction. Treat underlying disorder (SIADH = fluid restriction, DI = vasopressin). ODS irreversible; prevention critical.
